sites.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Diablo Lake
sites.capacity: Large road campground, roughly 90-100 numbered sites including walk-in tent sites and a group site; a smaller north loop sits across the highway
sites.water: Potable tap water during the serviced season; no supply in winter, when Thunder Arm and the creek are the only sources and need treating
sites.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. Fee campground, reservations through Recreation.gov for most of the season plus some first-come sites. No backcountry permit to sleep here — but one IS needed the moment you move uphill onto Colonial, Pyramid or Snowfield.
sites.notes: The practical staging ground for the whole west end of the corridor: directly under Colonial Peak and a short drive from the Pyramid Lake and Thunder Creek trailheads. Because it lies west of the usual winter gate at the Ross Dam trailhead, a handful of walk-in sites normally stay reachable through winter with no services and no fee — though a gate moved down to Newhalem would cut that off. Treat serviced opening and closing dates as approximate; they shift with snow and staffing. Arriving late on a summer Friday without a reservation is a poor plan.

sites.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
sites.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites
sites.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
sites.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. Sources disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.

sites.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy
sites.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out
sites.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
sites.notes: Parties heading for Snowfield sometimes push past the basin and sleep at the pass above the Colonial Glacier to shorten summit day and get onto the Neve Glacier early. The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.

sites.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
sites.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties
sites.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
sites.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
sites.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley. It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.

sites.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
sites.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it
sites.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
sites.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
sites.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.

sites.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
sites.capacity: Dispersed; a few flat spots at the lakes and a hidden pocket among the trees, enough for one or two parties
sites.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
sites.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit. Jerry Lakes sit on the Forest Service side of that divide — but if your route wanders west you have changed agencies. Carry both or confirm against the boundary before you go.
sites.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. No elevation is recorded because no confident figure was sourced. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
